meta.name: Imaging
meta.about: Imaging studies: how each modality works, what it shows well and badly, radiation and preparation. Educational, not a guide to which scan an individual should have.

x-ray.name: X-ray
x-ray.summary: The oldest and most widely available imaging test: a brief beam of X-rays casts a shadow picture of bone, air and soft tissue, ideal for fractures, chest infections and dental checks.
x-ray.how: A brief pulse of X-rays passes through the body onto a digital detector. Dense tissue such as bone absorbs most of the beam and appears white; air absorbs almost none and appears black; soft tissue and fluid are shades of grey in between. The image is a two-dimensional shadow of everything in the beam's path. The person lies or stands so that the body part is positioned against the detector, is asked to keep still and sometimes to hold their breath for a moment, and feels nothing: the exposure lasts a fraction of a second and the whole procedure usually takes a few minutes. The radiographer steps behind a screen to take the image, and machines are set to deliver the smallest amount of radiation needed to produce it; a lead apron or shield may be placed over parts of the body not being imaged, particularly in children. A radiologist or a reporting radiographer then reviews the images and sends a report to the clinician who requested them. Most X-rays are taken in hospital; dental X-rays are usually taken at the dental surgery.
shows: Bone: fractures, dislocations, arthritis, bone tumours and infection
Chest: pneumonia, fluid, collapsed lung, heart size, tumours
Abdomen: bowel obstruction, free air from a perforation, some stones
Teeth and jaw
Foreign bodies made of metal or glass
Dental: bitewing, periapical and panoramic views for decay, impacted wisdom teeth, jaw problems and implant planning; digital dental imaging uses less radiation than older film methods
bestFor: A first look at bones and the chest: fast, cheap and available everywhere
Following fracture healing
Bowel obstruction and perforation as a screen
notFor: Soft tissues such as ligaments, cartilage, brain and spinal cord
Early stress fractures and small bone injuries (MRI or CT)
Subtle lung disease (CT)
Anyone who is or might be pregnant unless it is an emergency, and repeat imaging in children without a clear clinical reason, since the young are more sensitive to radiation
x-ray.preparation: None for a standard X-ray. Jewellery, hair clips, bras and clothing with zips or metal poppers are removed from the area because metal shows on the image, and a gown is provided if needed. Anyone who is or might be pregnant, or who is breastfeeding, tells the radiographer beforehand, as does anyone with allergies or a previous reaction to contrast, since the NHS does not usually recommend X-rays in pregnancy except in an emergency. For contrast studies such as barium examinations the person may be asked to fast for a few hours or to stop certain medicines, and will be told in advance.
x-ray.duration: A few minutes in the room; the exposure itself lasts a fraction of a second. There are no after-effects from a standard X-ray and normal activities resume straight away; the requesting clinician explains when and how the result will be given.
x-ray.dose: Low. UKHSA publishes typical effective doses for each X-ray examination together with the equivalent period of natural background radiation and the associated lifetime risk: a chest film is among the lowest-dose examinations, equivalent to a few days of the background radiation everyone receives from the ground, building materials, food and space, while films of the hip, lumbar spine and pelvis deliver more. UKHSA has run national surveys of patient doses from radiography and fluoroscopy since 1986 and sets national diagnostic reference levels that departments compare themselves against. The FDA notes that a CT delivers a far higher dose than a conventional radiograph.
x-ray.risks: The radiation dose from a single film is tiny and the main theoretical risk is a very slightly increased chance of cancer later in life: X-rays are ionising radiation with enough energy to damage DNA, so the FDA treats every exposure as adding a small amount to lifetime risk while judging that, when an examination is appropriate, the benefit far outweighs it. The risk is lower for a chest, arm or foot X-ray than for a hip, spine or pelvis film, is greater the younger the patient (children and the unborn are more radiosensitive, and women receiving the same dose carry a somewhat higher risk than men), and is managed by justifying each request, keeping doses as low as reasonably achievable and shielding where useful. The abdomen and pelvis are avoided in pregnancy unless the examination is essential. There are no after-effects from a standard X-ray.
x-ray.contrast: Barium swallows and enemas coat the gut to outline it on fluoroscopy; iodine contrast is used for joints (arthrogram) and blood vessels (angiography). For these studies the NHS asks about allergies and any previous reaction to barium or contrast medium, and may ask the person to fast or to stop certain medicines beforehand.

commonUses.use: Cough, breathlessness, chest pain, fever, suspected pneumonia or heart failure
Injury, joint pain, suspected fracture, osteoarthritis
Obstruction, perforation, swallowed objects
DEXA scanning uses two low-energy X-ray beams to measure bone mineral density for osteoporosis

ct-scan.name: CT scan
ct-scan.summary: A rotating X-ray tube and computer build cross-sectional slices of the body in seconds, showing bone, organs, blood vessels and bleeding in fine detail; the workhorse of emergency imaging.
ct-scan.how: An X-ray tube spins around the body while it moves through the ring, collecting thousands of projections that a computer reconstructs into thin cross-sectional slices. The slices are stacked to view any plane or a 3D model. Iodine contrast injected into a vein lights up blood vessels and shows how organs and tumours take up blood. In practice the person lies on a flat bed that moves through the ring-shaped scanner while the radiographer operates it from an adjoining room, able to hear and speak to them throughout; they are asked to keep still and sometimes to breathe in, breathe out or hold their breath for a few seconds, because movement blurs the slices. The FDA describes CT as a tool for diagnosing disease, trauma and abnormality, guiding procedures and monitoring treatment such as cancer therapy, and notes that the detail it provides can sometimes make exploratory surgery unnecessary. Most newer scanners can lower the radiation dose, and UK departments compare the doses they deliver against national diagnostic reference levels published by UKHSA.
shows: Brain: bleeding, stroke (once established), tumours, injury
Chest: lung nodules and cancer, blood clots in the lung arteries (CTPA), fibrosis, infection
Abdomen and pelvis: appendicitis, diverticulitis, kidney stones, tumours, abscesses, bowel obstruction
Bones: complex fractures, the spine and pelvis
Blood vessels: aneurysms, dissection, coronary artery narrowing (CT coronary angiography)
bestFor: Emergencies where speed matters: trauma, stroke, suspected bleeding, severe abdominal pain
Lung disease and cancer staging
Kidney stones (no contrast needed)
Detailed bone anatomy for surgical planning
Guiding biopsies, drains and other procedures, and monitoring the response of cancer to treatment
notFor: Early stroke (may look normal for hours), spinal cord, ligaments and cartilage (MRI)
Repeated scans in children and young adults where dose accumulates
People with severe kidney disease or contrast allergy (contrast may be withheld)

Reassurance scans without a clear question: the FDA's principles of justification and optimisation mean a CT is performed only when it is medically warranted and a test using less or no radiation would be less appropriate, and then at the lowest dose that answers the question
ct-scan.preparation: Fasting for a few hours before contrast; kidney function checked; a cannula placed. Oral contrast is sometimes drunk an hour before abdominal scans. Before the scan, staff ask about the possibility of pregnancy, kidney problems, allergies and any previous reaction to contrast, and metal objects and clothing with metal fastenings are removed from the area being scanned. Children are generally scanned only for serious conditions because they are more sensitive to radiation, and a different exam that uses less or no radiation is chosen when it would answer the question as well.
ct-scan.duration: The scan itself takes seconds to a few minutes; the NHS says the whole scan usually takes about 10 to 20 minutes, and a visit is typically 20-30 minutes. People given contrast may be asked to wait around 30 minutes afterwards so that staff can check for a reaction before they leave.
ct-scan.dose: Considerably more than a plain X-ray. The FDA puts the adult effective dose from a head CT at roughly that of 100 chest X-rays, and UKHSA's patient-dose tables list an abdomen-pelvis CT at around 10 mSv: several years of natural background radiation. The dose depends on the body region, the protocol and the scanner, modern machines use far less than older ones, and departments benchmark their doses against UKHSA's national diagnostic reference levels. For a medically necessary scan the FDA judges the risk quite small when set against the benefit of an accurate diagnosis.
ct-scan.risks: A small increase in lifetime cancer risk with each scan, weighed against the benefit; the risk is larger in children and young adults, both because cancer risk per unit dose is higher at younger ages and because there is a longer lifetime for an effect to appear, and it accumulates with repeated scans. Tissue effects such as skin reddening or cataracts do not occur at the exposures used for CT. Contrast reactions are rare but can occasionally be severe (weakness, sweating or trouble breathing are reported at once), a temporary fall in kidney function occurs very rarely and mostly in people with known kidney disease, and contrast sometimes leaks from the vein at the injection site causing local pain and redness; an itchy rash can appear up to a week later. Unexpected incidental findings may lead to further, sometimes invasive, tests. Avoided in pregnancy unless there is an urgent medical reason.
ct-scan.contrast: Iodine-based, injected into a vein for vessels, organs and tumours; causes a warm flush and a metallic taste. Metformin may be paused around the scan. The NHS describes a warm feeling, a metallic taste and a sensation of needing to pass urine that settles within minutes. People are often advised to drink plenty of fluids for the rest of the day, and to report a rash or itching that appears in the days after the scan.

commonUses.use: Head injury, sudden severe headache, first seizure, suspected stroke or bleed
Lung cancer staging, pulmonary embolism (CTPA), fibrosis, complicated pneumonia
Severe pain, suspected appendicitis, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, cancer staging
CT coronary angiography for stable chest pain; calcium scoring

mri.name: MRI scan
mri.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not radiation, to produce detailed pictures of soft tissue: the brain, spinal cord, joints, muscles and organs.
mri.how: A powerful magnet aligns the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water and fat. Radio pulses knock them out of alignment and, as they relax back, they emit faint signals that differ by tissue type. Different pulse sequences (T1, T2, diffusion, fat suppression) emphasise different properties, giving unrivalled soft-tissue contrast without ionising radiation. The NHS likens the magnet's effect to a compass: lying inside the scanner lines the body's protons up, brief radio pulses knock them out of line, and because protons in different tissues realign at different speeds the returning signals let the computer tell tissues apart. The FDA notes that MRI can image any part of the body in any plane and separates fat, water, muscle and other soft tissue more clearly than CT, which is usually better for bone. The person lies on a narrow table that slides into the tunnel of the scanner, hears loud thumping and knocking during each sequence, and can speak to the radiographer through an intercom at any time; the operator can see and hear them throughout.
shows: Brain and spinal cord: stroke within minutes (diffusion), multiple sclerosis, tumours, epilepsy foci, dementia patterns
Spine: disc herniation, nerve compression, infection, cord injury
Joints: cartilage, menisci, ligaments, tendons, bone marrow oedema (early stress fractures)
Heart: muscle scar, cardiomyopathy, congenital disease
Liver, pancreas, bile ducts (MRCP), prostate, pelvis, breast
bestFor: Any question about the brain, spinal cord or nerves
Ligament, cartilage and tendon injuries of the knee, shoulder and ankle
Characterising liver, pancreatic and prostate lesions
Children and pregnancy, where radiation is avoided
notFor: Emergencies needing speed (a scan takes 20-60 minutes and the environment is hard to monitor)
Lungs and calcified structures (few hydrogen nuclei; CT is better)
People with certain implants, severe claustrophobia, or who cannot lie still
People who cannot be screened reliably for metal or implants, since the static field pulls ferromagnetic objects with force and some implants may heat, move or malfunction
mri.preparation: A detailed safety questionnaire about implants, metal fragments, pacemakers and previous surgery; all metal removed; ear protection for the loud knocking. Fasting for some abdominal scans. Everything metal comes off before entering the scan room: jewellery, hearing aids, watches, phones, keys, coins and wallets, and clothing with metal poppers or zips is swapped for a gown. The team is told in advance about any pacemaker or implant, metal fragments such as shrapnel or metal in the eye, kidney disease (relevant if gadolinium contrast is planned), tattoos (older inks may contain metal that heats or pulls) and any possibility of pregnancy. People who fear enclosed spaces say so beforehand: a sedative, or an open scanner, may be offered.
mri.duration: 20-60 minutes lying still inside a tube; each sequence lasts a few minutes. Longer examinations deposit more radiofrequency energy, so scan time is itself part of safety planning.
mri.dose: No ionising radiation. The NHS notes there is no conclusive evidence that exposure to the scanner's magnetic field causes harm or side effects, and the FDA states that there are no known cumulative risks from routine MRI, while adding that the long-term effects of very high field strengths are not yet known.
mri.risks: Ferromagnetic objects become projectiles; older pacemakers, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and metal in the eye can be dangerous. Gadolinium contrast is avoided in severe kidney disease and pregnancy. Claustrophobia is the commonest problem. The FDA lists further hazards that screening and good practice are designed to prevent: anything ferromagnetic, from keys to oxygen cylinders, becomes a projectile in the static field; devices or materials that conduct electricity (metallic objects, pulse oximeter leads, ECG leads and some tattoo pigments) can cause burns; radiofrequency energy warms the body, more so in long scans; the rapidly switching gradient fields are loud enough to damage hearing without ear protection and can produce a harmless light-touch or twitching sensation on the skin; and some people feel transient dizziness, nausea, headache, a metallic taste or flashes of light that fade on leaving the magnet. Scanners also hold large volumes of liquid helium, so scan rooms are fitted with oxygen monitors. Pregnant people tell the team before scanning so that the need for the scan can be weighed.
mri.contrast: Gadolinium, injected into a vein, highlights tumours, inflammation and blood vessels; rare allergic reactions. Kidney function is asked about beforehand because gadolinium is avoided or used cautiously in severe kidney disease.

commonUses.use: Stroke, tumours, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, dementia, headache with red flags
Sciatica with weakness, suspected cauda equina, infection, myelopathy
Ligament and meniscal tears, rotator cuff tears, cartilage
Liver lesions, bile duct stones (MRCP), prostate cancer, endometriosis, rectal cancer staging

ultrasound.name: Ultrasound
ultrasound.summary: High-frequency sound waves bounced off tissue give real-time, radiation-free images, used for pregnancy, the abdomen, the heart (echocardiography), blood vessels and guiding needles.
ultrasound.how: A hand-held probe sends pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes from tissue boundaries. The depth of each echo builds a live moving image. Doppler ultrasound measures the frequency shift from moving blood to show flow direction and speed in colour. It is safe, portable and real-time, but sound cannot cross bone or air. Because the images are captured in real time, the FDA notes, ultrasound also shows movement: the beating heart, bowel and blood flowing through vessels. The scan is usually performed by a sonographer or a radiologist. A clear, water-based gel is spread on the skin so the probe makes good contact, the room is dimmed to make the screen easier to see, and the operator presses and angles the probe and may ask the person to turn on their side, breathe in or hold their breath for a better view. For the pelvis an internal (transvaginal) probe may be offered for more detailed images, with consent and a chaperone present. A report is written afterwards and sent to the doctor who requested the scan; results are not usually given during the appointment, except for some pregnancy scans.
shows: Abdomen: gallstones, liver size and texture, kidney obstruction, aortic aneurysm, fluid
Pelvis: pregnancy, ovaries and uterus, bladder volume, prostate (transrectal)
Vessels: deep vein thrombosis, carotid narrowing, varicose veins, arterial blockages
Heart: the echocardiogram
Soft tissue: thyroid nodules, breast lumps, lymph nodes, tendons, muscle tears, abscesses
Guidance for needles: biopsies, drains, injections, cannulas
Pregnancy: how far along the pregnancy is, the fetal heartbeat, the number of babies and, at the NHS 20-week screening scan, the baby's anatomy
bestFor: First test for the gallbladder, kidneys, thyroid, scrotum, pregnancy and leg veins
Any test that must be repeated or done at the bedside
Guiding procedures in real time
Children and pregnancy
notFor: Anything behind bone (brain in adults, spinal cord) or air (lungs beyond the surface, gas-filled bowel)
Deep structures in larger patients (image quality falls with depth)
A comprehensive survey: it shows what the operator points at, so quality depends on skill
Non-medical 'keepsake' fetal videos, which the FDA discourages
ultrasound.preparation: Depends on the area. For the abdomen, liver or gallbladder the person is usually asked not to eat for several hours beforehand (water is allowed) so the gallbladder is full and the stomach empty; for the pelvis, kidneys and bladder a full bladder is needed, so a set amount of water is drunk before arriving and not passed until after the scan; early pregnancy scans need a full bladder while later ones need none. Scans of the neck, limbs, veins and soft tissue need no preparation. The appointment letter gives the specific instructions.
ultrasound.duration: Typically 10 to 40 minutes depending on the area examined; Doppler studies of blood flow and some pregnancy scans take longer. The gel is wiped off at the end and the person can eat, drink and carry on as normal.
ultrasound.dose: No ionising radiation. The FDA notes that diagnostic ultrasound has been in medical use for decades and, being non-ionising, does not carry the risks of X-ray-based imaging; the NHS states that standard diagnostic ultrasound has no known harmful effects.
ultrasound.risks: None known at diagnostic settings; brief discomfort from probe pressure on a tender area, and some discomfort from a full bladder or an internal probe. The FDA notes that ultrasound can heat tissue slightly and in some cases produce small gas pockets in fluids or tissue (cavitation), that the long-term consequences of these effects are not known, and that it is therefore considered safe when used prudently by trained operators; it advises prudent use in pregnancy and discourages non-medical 'keepsake' fetal videos. The main practical limitation is that image quality depends on the operator and on the person's build.
ultrasound.contrast: Microbubble contrast (tiny gas bubbles injected into a vein) improves characterisation of liver and kidney lesions.

commonUses.use: Gallstones, jaundice, abnormal liver tests
Early pregnancy and its location, fibroids, ovarian cysts, the endometrium after bleeding; transvaginal for detail
Kidney injury, obstruction, stones, bladder emptying
Suspected deep vein thrombosis
Thyroid nodules, lymph nodes, carotid stenosis after a stroke
Tendon tears, joint effusions, guiding steroid injections

pet-scan.name: PET-CT scan
pet-scan.summary: Positron emission tomography tracks a mildly radioactive sugar or tracer to show where cells are most active, usually combined with CT to stage cancer and check treatment response.
pet-scan.how: A tiny amount of a radioactive tracer is injected and the scanner detects where it accumulates. The commonest tracer, FDG, is a glucose analogue, so tissues that burn a lot of sugar (most cancers, infection, inflammation, the brain and heart) light up. The PET image is fused with a CT taken at the same time to show exactly where the activity sits. Other nuclear medicine scans use tracers that go to bone, the thyroid, the heart muscle or the kidneys. MedlinePlus describes PET as a nuclear imaging test that shows how well tissues and organs are working rather than only what they look like, and the National Cancer Institute defines a nuclear medicine scan as one in which a radioactive substance locates and binds to specific cells or tissues, including cancer cells, so that a camera can map it. FDG is labelled with fluorine-18, which emits positrons; the scanner detects the resulting radiation and a computer turns it into three-dimensional pictures. Because tumours usually metabolise glucose faster than normal tissue they take up more FDG and stand out, but inflamed tissue also accumulates it, so the scan is read alongside the CT and the clinical history. During the scan the person lies on a narrow table that moves slowly through the ring of the scanner and must keep very still, since movement blurs the images; an intercom allows them to speak to staff at any time. Nuclear medicine also treats disease: radioactive substances are used to treat some thyroid cancers and lymphomas.
shows: Cancer: staging, finding spread, judging response to treatment, distinguishing scar from active tumour
Infection and inflammation of unknown source, vasculitis, infected grafts
Brain: dementia patterns, epilepsy foci
Heart: viable versus scarred muscle
Bone scan: metastases, stress fractures, infection, Paget disease
Thyroid uptake scan: overactive nodules versus thyroiditis
Cancer in practice: in non-small-cell lung cancer, integrated PET-CT has become a standard test for staging the primary tumour, lymph nodes and distant spread, and for assessing response to treatment
bestFor: Whole-body cancer staging in lung cancer, lymphoma, melanoma, oesophageal and head and neck cancer
Deciding whether a lung nodule is likely malignant
Fever of unknown origin
notFor: Cancers with low glucose uptake (some prostate, kidney, low-grade and well-differentiated tumours; other tracers are used)
Very small tumours, for which sensitivity falls sharply, partly because of breathing movement during the scan
Brain metastases (the brain glows with normal uptake; MRI instead)
Telling cancer from inflammation on its own, since FDG also accumulates in inflamed and infected tissue
Uncontrolled diabetes, which spoils FDG uptake
pet-scan.preparation: Fast for 6 hours, drinking only water, avoid exercise for 24 hours, keep warm; blood glucose checked, and people with diabetes may need their medicines adjusted because they interfere with the result. Metal items such as jewellery are left off. About an hour before the scan the tracer is injected into a vein in the arm or hand (a brief sting from the needle; the scan itself is painless) and the person then rests quietly while it distributes; some centres ask them not to read, talk or use a phone during this period because muscle activity changes where the tracer goes.
pet-scan.duration: About 2-3 hours in the department. The tracer is given about an hour before imaging; the NHS puts the scan itself at around 30 to 60 minutes, with the person lying still for about 30 minutes of that. Results usually reach the referring doctor within 1 to 2 weeks after a radiologist has reported the images.
pet-scan.dose: Moderate. MedlinePlus puts the radiation from a PET scan at about the same amount as most CT scans, and the CT component adds to it (a low-dose localising CT contributes less than a full diagnostic CT). The NHS describes the tracer as a small amount of radiation that drops to a safe level quickly and has gone from the body within a few hours; it leaves in the urine and stool, which is why fluids are encouraged afterwards.
pet-scan.risks: Radiation as above; the NHS and MedlinePlus advise limiting close contact with pregnant women and small children for a period after the tracer, usually up to a day. Allergic reactions to FDG are very rare. There is no recovery time unless a sedative was given, and most people go home soon after the scan. As with any sensitive test, uptake in inflammation or infection can mimic cancer and lead to further tests.
pet-scan.contrast: The radiotracer itself; the CT component may be low-dose without contrast or a full diagnostic scan with iodine.

commonUses.use: Staging and restaging cancer, planning radiotherapy
Characterising a lung nodule; mediastinal lymph nodes
Frontotemporal versus Alzheimer dementia; amyloid PET
Bone scan for metastases or occult fracture

mammography.name: Mammography
mammography.summary: A low-dose X-ray of the compressed breast that can detect cancers years before they can be felt, used for screening programmes and for investigating breast symptoms.
mammography.how: A low-dose X-ray of each breast, compressed between two plates for a few seconds to spread the tissue thin and hold it still. Two views are taken of each side. Digital tomosynthesis takes a sweep of images to reconstruct thin slices, reducing overlap. Cancers show as masses, distortions or clusters of tiny calcifications, often years before they can be felt. At an NHS screening appointment a female mammographer positions one breast at a time on the machine; the person undresses from the waist up in private, the breast is pressed firmly between two clear plates for a few seconds, and the pressure both holds the breast still and lets the machine use the lowest radiation dose that still gives a clear image. The machine is then tilted for a side view and the other breast is imaged the same way. The images are read by radiologists or trained mammogram readers, who look for masses, deposits of calcium and the pattern of breast density; dense breast tissue makes a cancer harder to see. Diagnostic mammography, used when there is a symptom or a screening recall, takes images from more angles than a screening study and so delivers a somewhat higher dose. Digital breast tomosynthesis (3D mammography) combined with standard mammography finds more tumours than standard mammography alone, although whether it reduces breast cancer deaths is still being tested. In the United States, the Mammography Quality Standards Act requires every facility to be FDA-certified, surveyed annually by a medical physicist, inspected yearly, and to send each patient a plain-language result.
shows: Breast cancer, including ductal carcinoma in situ (calcifications)
Benign lumps: cysts, fibroadenomas (with ultrasound to tell them apart)
Breast density, which affects both risk and how easily cancers are seen
Reporting: in the United States results are graded with BI-RADS categories from 0 (more imaging needed) to 6 (known cancer); in England a screening result is either normal or a recall for assessment
bestFor: Population screening: in England women are invited every 3 years from a first invitation between 50 and 53 until their 71st birthday, and can continue to book screening themselves afterwards; US guidance (USPSTF) recommends screening every 2 years from 40 to 74

Investigating a new lump, nipple change or skin change in women over 40; trans women on long-term oestrogen and trans men who have not had chest surgery are offered screening on the same basis as the tissue they have
Follow-up after breast cancer treatment
Earlier or more frequent screening in women at high risk, such as carriers of harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants, usually alongside MRI
notFor: Younger women with dense breasts, where ultrasound and MRI see more
Assessing implants (MRI); implants can hide breast tissue, so the facility is told in advance and special implant-displacement views are used
Ruling out cancer completely: the NHS is clear that mammograms do not find all cancers, so a new lump or change is always investigated even after a normal screen
Preventing cancer: screening only finds cancer that is already present
mammography.preparation: No deodorant, antiperspirant or talc on the day (they can affect the images); book after a period if breasts are tender. Staff confirm identity and ask about any previous breast problems; necklaces and nipple piercings are removed, and a binder is taken off before the images. Anyone with implants tells the facility when booking.
mammography.duration: The NHS says the whole appointment should take no longer than about 30 minutes; the imaging itself takes only a few minutes, with each compression lasting a few seconds. Results are usually sent by letter within about 2 weeks and the GP is informed.
mammography.dose: Low. The NHS states that the amount of radiation used in a mammogram is very small and the health risk very low, and the compression that holds the breast still is what lets the machine use the lowest dose for a clear image. A diagnostic study, which takes more views, gives a somewhat higher dose than a two-view screening study.
mammography.risks: Discomfort from compression, which some people find briefly painful; it eases quickly and the mammographer can be asked to stop at any point. A very small radiation dose. False alarms: in England about 4 in every 100 women screened are called back for further tests (examination, more mammograms, ultrasound and sometimes a needle biopsy), and about 1 of those 4 is found to have cancer, so most recalls are not cancer. Overdiagnosis: some women are diagnosed and treated for a cancer that would never have been found otherwise and would not have become life-threatening. Missed cancers: a cancer may not be visible, or very occasionally is missed by the reader, which is why changes between screens are reported to a GP. Set against these, the NHS estimates that screening saves about 1,400 lives a year in England; it does not prevent breast cancer.
mammography.contrast: Contrast-enhanced mammography with iodine is an emerging alternative to breast MRI.

commonUses.use: Asymptomatic women in the screening age range (England: every 3 years from the first invitation at 50-53 until the 71st birthday)
Lump, discharge, dimpling, in a one-stop clinic with examination, ultrasound and needle biopsy
Earlier and yearly screening for BRCA carriers, usually with MRI

fluoroscopy.name: Fluoroscopy and angiography
fluoroscopy.summary: Continuous, low-dose X-ray imaging shown as a live moving picture, used to watch swallowing, guide catheters and joint injections and follow contrast through the gut or vessels.
fluoroscopy.how: A continuous or pulsed X-ray beam produces a moving image on a screen, so the radiologist can watch swallowing, bowel movement, joint motion or the passage of contrast through blood vessels in real time. Angiography injects iodine contrast through a fine catheter threaded into an artery, mapping the vessel tree and allowing treatment (angioplasty, stents, coiling, clot removal) in the same session. The beam is switched on only while the operator needs to see, and the FDA's guidance is that fluoroscopy is always performed with the lowest acceptable exposure for the shortest time necessary, because dose rises with screening time. For angiography the NHS describes numbing the skin at the groin or wrist, passing a thin catheter into the artery (the person may feel some pushing and pulling but it should not hurt), then injecting contrast while a series of X-rays is taken as it flows through the vessels; adults are usually awake, while young children may have a general anaesthetic. A barium swallow works the same way for the gullet: the person drinks a white barium liquid and the radiologist watches it pass in real time, and a videofluoroscopy (modified barium swallow) records foods and drinks of different textures mixed with barium, usually with a speech and language therapist present.
shows: Swallowing problems and reflux (barium or water-soluble swallow)
Bowel narrowing, fistulas, leaks after surgery
Blood vessel narrowing, blockage, aneurysms and bleeding points
Coronary arteries during cardiac catheterisation
Guiding the placement of tubes, lines, stents and orthopaedic hardware
Swallowing in detail: videofluoroscopy records how foods and drinks of different textures are swallowed and whether any enters the airway
bestFor: Anything that must be watched moving
Combining diagnosis and treatment in one sitting (interventional radiology and cardiology)
Checking that a catheter, wire or stent is in the right place
Guiding orthopaedic work such as joint replacement and fracture fixation, and placing stents and other devices
notFor: Routine diagnosis where a still image will do (X-ray, CT) because screening time adds dose
People who cannot cooperate with swallowing or positioning instructions
Pregnancy, unless the information is urgently needed: anyone who might be pregnant tells staff before the procedure
fluoroscopy.preparation: Fasting for gut studies and angiography; kidney function and clotting checked; blood thinners managed; a cannula for sedation. Before angiography the team takes a medical history, asks about allergies and current medicines, and says which, if any, should be stopped beforehand; anyone who might be pregnant tells staff in advance. Barium studies need an empty stomach, and a known barium allergy is declared; the appointment letter carries the specific instructions for each study.
fluoroscopy.duration: From around a quarter of an hour for a simple barium swallow (some gut studies take images at intervals over several hours) to 1-3 hours for complex interventional procedures. After angiography the person rests in a recovery area while the puncture site settles and usually goes home the same day, though an overnight stay is sometimes needed.
fluoroscopy.dose: Highly variable and governed by screening time. The FDA notes that fluoroscopy can deliver relatively high doses, especially in complex interventional procedures that need long fluoroscopy times, whereas the NHS describes the dose from a standard angiogram as small. UKHSA's patient-dose tables place barium studies of the bowel among the higher-dose diagnostic X-ray examinations, and UKHSA runs national dose surveys of fluoroscopy examinations so that departments can compare their practice against national reference levels. Skin can be injured after very prolonged screening.
fluoroscopy.risks: Radiation dose that rises with screening time: the FDA identifies two concerns, radiation injury to the skin and underlying tissue (a burn-like effect after long procedures) and a small possibility of a radiation-induced cancer later in life, adding that the probability of either from a single procedure is statistically very small, that the radiation risk is usually far smaller than the other risks of the procedure such as sedation, anaesthesia or the treatment itself, and that where there may be a high dose to the lens of the eye cataract is a further risk. Contrast reactions (a mild itchy rash is the usual form; anaphylaxis is very rare) and a usually temporary strain on the kidneys. For angiography, bruising, soreness and a small lump at the puncture site for days to weeks are common; less often the artery is damaged with internal bleeding that occasionally needs surgical repair, a pseudoaneurysm (a blood-filled bulge at the entry site) forms later and needs treatment, and rarely a heart attack or stroke occurs. Afterwards, bleeding from the puncture site that does not stop with pressure, severe pain, spreading redness or swelling, or a limb that turns pale or cold are reasons to contact the care team urgently.
fluoroscopy.contrast: Barium for the gut (or a water-soluble alternative if a leak is suspected); iodine for vessels, joints and the urinary tract. Barium is not digested, so stools are paler for a few days and constipation can follow, which is why plenty of fluids are advised afterwards. Iodine contrast can give a brief warm flush or a feeling of needing to pass urine, and because blood vessels do not show on ordinary X-rays no angiogram is possible without it.

commonUses.use: Coronary angiography for heart attack and angina, with angioplasty and stenting
Cerebral angiography for aneurysms; mechanical thrombectomy in stroke
Barium swallow for dysphagia; contrast studies after bowel surgery
Peripheral angiography and angioplasty for blocked leg arteries

dxa-scan.name: DXA scan (bone density)
dxa-scan.summary: A quick, very low-dose X-ray measurement of bone mineral density at the hip and spine, reported as a T-score, that diagnoses osteoporosis and estimates fracture risk.
dxa-scan.how: Two X-ray beams of different energies pass through the bone; the difference in how much each is absorbed gives the amount of mineral per area of bone. The scanner passes over the lower spine and hip while the person lies still on a padded table for about 10-20 minutes.
shows: Bone mineral density at the hip and lumbar spine, and sometimes the forearm
A T-score comparing the result with young healthy adults and a Z-score comparing it with people of the same age and sex
Change in density on repeat scans, to monitor treatment
bestFor: Diagnosing osteoporosis and osteopenia
Estimating fracture risk together with clinical risk factors (FRAX)
Deciding on and monitoring bone-protective treatment
Assessing bone loss from long-term corticosteroids or other causes
notFor: Finding the cause of bone or back pain
Detecting fractures, tumours or arthritis in detail: X-ray, CT or MRI do that
Children and people with spinal hardware, where interpretation needs specialist adjustment
dxa-scan.preparation: No calcium supplements on the day of the scan; wear clothes without metal; mention recent contrast X-rays or nuclear scans, which can interfere.
dxa-scan.dose: Very low: a fraction of a chest X-ray, less than a day of natural background radiation.
dxa-scan.risks: Minimal radiation exposure; not done in pregnancy unless essential.

commonUses.use: Bone density for osteoporosis diagnosis and fracture risk
When hip or spine cannot be measured, or in hyperparathyroidism
Body composition (fat and lean mass) in specialist settings
